deltas.afterRequirement: Explain the fictional known-source lineage and once-only descendant result with its alias and non-erasure limits; offer three optional reproduction/inspection tasks with actual shared setup, exact commands and expected one selected passing test, followed by substantive matched explanations for trailing-LF edge trimming versus fixed raw counts and preserved internal LF, policy order/identity and known descendants.
deltas.afterValue: Optional practice: inspect the recorded evidence Source withdrawal is a known-lineage calculation Filtering also preserves source lineage so a later withdrawal can identify recorded downstream artifacts. The separate fictional graph uses r0 as a raw-source node alias, not as the worked table’s record label or an actual occurrence digest. Its descendants are a0, f0, s0, tok0 and w0. Two paths reach w0; the result lists it once. The unrelated branch f9 belongs to a different source and is not in this withdrawal’s descendant set. Validate the supplied lineage graph, then list each known descendant of the selected raw source once; this does not erase stored data. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/deletion.rs#known-descendant-withdrawal pub fn withdrawal( &self, raw_roots: &[String], limits: GraphLimits, ) -> Result<WithdrawalPlan, DataError> { let kinds = self.validate(limits)?; let mut reached = BTreeSet::new(); let mut pending = BTreeSet::new(); for root in raw_roots { if kinds.get(root.as_str()) != Some(&NodeKind::RawSource) { return Err(DataError::InvalidGraph("unknown or non-source root")); } pending.insert(root.as_str()); } while let Some(id) = pending.pop_first() { if !reached.insert(id) { continue; } for edge in &self.edges { if edge.parent == id && !reached.contains(edge.child.as_str()) { pending.insert(edge.child.as_str()); } } } let mut artifacts = Vec::new(); let mut sources = Vec::new(); for id in reached { match kinds.get(id) { Some(NodeKind::RawSource) => sources.push(id.into()), Some(NodeKind::Artifact) => artifacts.push(id.into()), None => return Err(DataError::InvalidGraph("unknown reached node")), } } Ok(WithdrawalPlan { artifacts, sources }) } Run these commands from the repository root with Docker installed and running. Each selects exactly one test; expect one passing test, not zero selected tests. Reproduce the fixture’s byte accounting. Inspect the assertions linking payload, delimiter, decoded and normalized byte totals. COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering --test corpus_filtering fixture_counts_and_byte_conservation -- --exact Reproduce the comparison that places the manual-marker rule before the secret-marker rule. Inspect the first terminal decision for r7 and the identities compared by the test. COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering --test corpus_filtering swapping_secret_and_review_changes_first_terminal -- --exact Reproduce the known-lineage withdrawal. Inspect the assertions checking the sorted, duplicate-free descendant set. COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo test --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering --test corpus_filtering withdrawal_reaches_known_descendants_once -- --exact Checked explanations for the three reproduction tasks The trailing LF byte in each decoded fixture payload remains part of the raw payload and physical source byte counts, but normalization trims it from the end of the decoded text. Internal LF characters remain unchanged. Trimming the trailing LF changes the normalized byte count, not the number of bytes read from the raw source. With the secret-marker rule first, r7 is rejected and never reaches the manual-marker rule. With the manual-marker rule first, r7 is held for review and never reaches the secret-marker rule. The raw source and occurrence identities do not change. The derived policy and artifact identities change because the ordered filtering policy is different. The descendant set contains a0, f0, s0, tok0 and w0, with w0 listed once despite its two incoming paths; it excludes the unrelated f9. This calculation neither deletes stored bytes nor unlearns a trained model. It cannot discover unrecorded copies. The graph’s checkpoint-like node is fictional; this example has not trained a model.
